subject: Medicine
topic: Warm vs Cold Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia Coombs and Rituximab
stem: A 64-year-old woman with a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) presents with a 2-week history of fatigue, dark tea-colored urine, and painful, dusky-blue, purplish discoloration of her earlobes, nose tip, fingers, and toes that occurs whenever she is exposed to cold ambient temperatures (acrocyanosis / Raynaud-like phenomenon). The discoloration resolves completely upon warming. Physical examination reveals conjunctival pallor and mild scleral icterus. There is no splenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL (baseline 11.8 g/dL), MCV 108 fL, reticulocyte count 8.4%, total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL (indirect bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL), serum LDH 1,640 U/L (normal 140-280 U/L), and serum haptoglobin < 10 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear demonstrates prominent RBC AGGLUTINATION (erythrocytes clumping in large clusters resembling grape bunches at room temperature) that disperses when the slide is gently warmed to 37°C. Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT / Direct Coombs test) is STRONGLY POSITIVE FOR C3D COMPLEMENT ONLY, AND COMPLETELY NEGATIVE FOR IGG. Cold agglutinin titer is elevated at 1:1,024. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this patient?

options.text: Avoidance of cold exposure (thermal protection), warm intravenous fluids and blood warmers if transfusions are needed, and initiation of rituximab monotherapy
options.explanation: AUTOIMMUNE HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA (AIHA) is divided into two distinct clinical and immunological entities: (1) WARM AUTOIMMUNE HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA (wAIHA, 80-90% of cases): Mediated by IGG AUTOANTIBODIES that bind RBC surface antigens (Rh complex) at core body temperature (37°C). IgG-coated RBCs are partially phagocytosed by splenic macrophages via Fc-gamma receptors, forming SPHEROCYTES that undergo EXTRAVASCULAR HEMOLYSIS in the spleen. DAT is positive for IgG (or IgG + C3d). First-line therapy is SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROIDS (oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day); SPLENECTOMY or rituximab is second-line. (2) COLD AGGLUTININ DISEASE (CAD, 10-20% of cases): Mediated by IGM AUTOANTIBODIES that bind erythrocyte I/i carbohydrate antigens at cold temperatures (< 30°C) in peripheral capillary beds (fingers, toes, ears, nose). Pentameric IgM cross-links erythrocytes, causing ERYTHROCYTE AGGLUTINATION (microvascular sludging producing painful acrocyanosis). When IgM binds, it fixes the C1 complement complex. As erythrocytes return to the warmer core circulation (37°C), IgM dissociates, but C3b remains covalently bound to the RBC surface. C3b is degraded to C3d. DAT IS CHARACTERISTICALLY POSITIVE FOR C3D ONLY, AND COMPLETELY NEGATIVE FOR IGG. Extravascular clearance occurs in hepatic Kupffer cells via C3b receptors (or terminal intravascular C5b-9 MAC lysis). MANAGEMENT OF COLD AGGLUTININ DISEASE: (a) FIRST-LINE NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL: AVOID COLD EXPOSURE (thermal insulation, hats, gloves, warming all IV fluids and blood products); (b) FIRST-LINE MEDICAL PHARMACOTHERAPY: RITUXIMAB (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) is the drug of choice, achieving high response rates by suppressing clonal B cells. (SUTIMLIMAB, a C1s inhibitor, is approved for severe disease). CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATIONS IN COLD AGGLUTININ DISEASE: CORTICOSTEROIDS ARE COMPLETELY INEFFECTIVE (response rate < 10%), and SPLENECTOMY IS USELESS (because hemolysis occurs in the liver via C3b, not in the spleen via IgG Fc).

options.text: High-dose oral prednisone 1 mg/kg daily as the primary first-line therapeutic agent
options.explanation: Corticosteroids are first-line for Warm AIHA, but are completely ineffective in Cold Agglutinin Disease (< 10% response) and should not be used as primary therapy.

options.text: Immediate emergency laparoscopic splenectomy to eliminate the primary site of red cell destruction
options.explanation: Splenectomy works for Warm AIHA (splenic extravascular clearance), but fails in Cold Agglutinin Disease because C3b-opsonized erythrocytes are cleared in the liver by Kupffer cells.

options.text: Perform an emergent exchange blood transfusion using unwashed, room-temperature packed red blood cells
options.explanation: Transfusing unwashed blood without a blood warmer in cold agglutinin disease precipitates massive intravascular agglutination, shock, and catastrophic hemolysis; blood must be warmed to 37°C.

options.text: Administration of daily oral methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine
options.explanation: Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine treat autoimmune connective tissue diseases; they have no role in cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia.

subject: Surgery
topic: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma Medical Regimen and Laser Iridotomy
stem: A 64-year-old hyperopic woman presents to the emergency department with a 3-hour history of sudden-onset, excruciating right eye and right frontal headache that began while watching a movie in a darkened cinema. The pain is severe, aching, and accompanied by nausea, two episodes of vomiting, and blurred vision with prominent 'rainbow-colored halos' around streetlights. Physical examination reveals an agonizingly uncomfortable woman holding her right eye. Visual acuity is reduced to 20/200 in the right eye (baseline 20/25) and 20/25 in the left eye. Slit-lamp and penlight examination of the right eye demonstrates severe ciliary flush (conjunctival injection concentrated around the limbus), a hazy, 'steamy' edematous cornea, a shallow anterior chamber, and a MID-DILATED, FIXED, NON-REACTIVE PUPIL (5 mm, non-responsive to direct or consensual light). The right globe feels rock-hard to palpation compared to the soft left globe. Tonometry reveals an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 62 mm Hg in the right eye (normal 10-21 mm Hg) and 16 mm Hg in the left eye. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate medical management combination before definitive surgical intervention?

options.text: Administration of topical tropicamide and cyclopentolate mydriatic drops to dilate the pupil and release posterior synechiae
options.explanation: Mydriatic/cycloplegic drops (tropicamide, atropine) dilate the pupil, which further crowds the iridocorneal angle and worsens pupillary block; mydriatics are strictly contraindicated in angle closure.

options.text: Immediate topical ocular hypotensive drops (timolol, apraclonidine, and pilocarpine) combined with systemic intravenous acetazolamide (or IV mannitol)
options.explanation: ACUTE ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA (AACG) is an ophthalmic emergency that can result in permanent, irreversible vision loss (ischemic optic neuropathy) within 24 to 48 hours if left untreated. It occurs in anatomically predisposed eyes (hyperopia / farsightedness, shallow anterior chamber, thick crystalline lens, advanced age, female sex, Inuit/Asian ethnicity). The trigger is PUPILLARY DILATION (mydriasis occurring in dim lighting, emotional stress, or after sympathomimetic / anticholinergic medications like atropine, pseudoephedrine, or diphenhydramine). Mid-dilation brings the peripheral iris into contact with the lens (PUPIL BLOCK). Aqueous humor secreted by the ciliary body cannot flow from the posterior chamber through the pupil into the anterior chamber. The trapped fluid builds up in the posterior chamber, bowing the peripheral iris forward ('iris bombé') and completely occluding the trabecular meshwork in the iridocorneal drainage angle. This causes a precipitous, extreme spike in INTRAOCULAR PRESSURE (IOP, often 50-80 mm Hg). Clinical tetrad: (1) Severe ocular pain and frontal headache with nausea/vomiting; (2) Blurred vision with 'rainbow halos' around lights; (3) Ciliary injection and cloudy 'steamy' cornea; (4) FIXED, MID-DILATED PUPIL and ROCK-HARD GLOBE. stem: A 52-year-old man is hospitalized on the orthopedic service following open reduction and internal fixation of a bimalleolar ankle fracture. On postoperative day 3 (approximately 72 hours after his last alcoholic drink), he becomes acutely agitated, diaphoretic, and confused. He shouts at imaginary insects crawling across his bedsheets and tries to pull out his intravenous lines. He has a 25-year history of consuming 12 to 15 beers daily. Physical examination reveals an agitated, tremulous man drenched in perspiration. Vital signs: blood pressure 184/108 mm Hg, heart rate 136/min, respirations 24/min, and core temperature 38.6°C (101.5°F). Neurological examination reveals marked coarse bilateral postural tremor of his outstretched hands, bilateral horizontal nystagmus, dilated pupils, and severe psychomotor agitation. He is disoriented to time, date, and hospital location, and cannot state his surgeon's name. Complete blood count shows MCV 102 fL, and liver profile demonstrates: AST 142 U/L, ALT 68 U/L (AST/ALT ratio > 2.0). Serum electrolytes and head CT are completely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate medical management strategy?

options.text: Administration of oral haloperidol 10 mg monotherapy and physical four-point restraints without benzodiazepines
options.explanation: Antipsychotic monotherapy is strictly contraindicated in alcohol withdrawal because neuroleptics lower the seizure threshold, worsen hyperthermia, and do not treat underlying GABA withdrawal.

options.text: Immediate administration of intravenous flumazenil to accelerate hepatic clearance of alcohol metabolites
options.explanation: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist that triggers immediate, intractable status epilepticus and death in alcohol withdrawal.

options.text: Symptom-triggered intravenous benzodiazepine therapy (such as diazepam or lorazepam) titrated to clinical response using the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA-Ar) protocol, combined with supportive intravenous hydration and thiamine
options.explanation: ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME results from neurochemical adaptation to chronic ethanol exposure: chronic alcohol stimulates inhibitory GABA-A receptors and inhibits excitatory NMDA glutamate receptors. With abrupt cessation of alcohol, the brain suffers a LOSS OF GABA-MEDIATED INHIBITION and a REBOUND EXCESS OF GLUTAMATERGIC NMDA EXCITATION. Clinical progression occurs in distinct timeframes following the last drink: (1) MILD WITHDRAWAL (6 to 24 hours): Tremor, insomnia, anxiety, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension; (2) WITHDRAWAL SEIZURES (12 to 48 hours): Generalized tonic-clonic convulsions; (3) ALCOHOLIC HALLUCINOSIS (12 to 48 hours): Auditory, visual, or tactile hallucinations WITH INTACT SENSORIUM (patient is oriented and vital signs are normal; not delirium); (4) DELIRIUM TREMENS (DT, 48 to 96 hours post-cessation): The most severe, life-threatening manifestation, carrying a 5% mortality. Diagnostic tetrad: (a) ACUTE DELIRIUM (fluctuating confusion, disorientation, severe inattention); (b) SEVERE AUTONOMIC HYPERACTIVITY (high fever, severe hypertension, marked tachycardia, profuse diaphoresis); (c) VIVID VISUAL OR TACTILE HALLUCINATIONS; (d) COARSE TREMOR AND AGITATION. Management: (1) BENZODIAZEPINES ARE THE CORNERSTONE OF THERAPY: Benzodiazepines act as cross-tolerant GABA-A receptor agonists, substituting for alcohol to restore central inhibitory tone, prevent seizures, and blunten autonomic hyperactivity. The standard of care is a SYMPTOM-TRIGGERED REGIMEN using the CIWA-Ar scale (administering IV DIAZEPAM or IV LORAZEPAM whenever CIWA-Ar >= 8-10). (LORAZEPAM or oxazepam are preferred in patients with severe hepatic cirrhosis due to lack of oxidative hepatic metabolism: mnemonic 'LOT': Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam). (2) THIAMINE (VITAMIN B1): High-dose IV thiamine MUST BE ADMINISTERED BEFORE ANY GLUCOSE INFUSIONS to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. (3) Supportive ICU care with IV fluids and electrolyte repletion. Antipsychotics (haloperidol) lower the seizure threshold and are avoided unless severe delirium persists despite adequate benzodiazepine sedation.

options.text: Administration of oral disulfiram 250 mg daily to deter future alcohol cravings
options.explanation: Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase and is used for abstinence maintenance in stable outpatients; giving it during active withdrawal is dangerous and ineffective.

options.text: Initiation of daily oral naltrexone and outpatient motivational interviewing with immediate hospital discharge
options.explanation: Delirium tremens is a medical emergency with up to 5% mortality requiring intensive care monitoring and IV benzodiazepines; discharging a patient with DT is fatal.

topic: Infective Endocarditis Antibiotic Prophylaxis High-Risk Criteria
stem: A 58-year-old man presents to his cardiologist for routine clearance prior to an extensive dental procedure. He is scheduled to undergo deep subgingival scaling, root planing, and tooth extraction for severe periodontal disease tomorrow morning. His cardiovascular medical history is notable for severe degenerative aortic stenosis, for which he underwent surgical aortic valve replacement with a mechanical bileaflet St. Jude prosthetic valve 4 years ago. He also has a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, for which he takes therapeutic warfarin (current INR 2.4). He has no history of previous infective endocarditis. Physical examination reveals an alert man with a crisp mechanical aortic closure click and a grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border. He has no fever, peripheral stigmata of endocarditis, or signs of heart failure. He has no known drug allergies. According to the American Heart Association (AHA) and American College of Cardiology (ACC) guidelines, which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis recommendation for this patient prior to his dental procedure?

options.text: No antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated because antibiotic prophylaxis does not prevent endocarditis in prosthetic valve recipients
options.explanation: Prosthetic heart valves carry the highest risk of catastrophic morbidity and mortality from endocarditis; antibiotic prophylaxis is explicitly indicated for dental gingival manipulation.

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days beginning 24 hours before the procedure
options.explanation: Prolonged multi-day antibiotic courses are obsolete and harmful; guidelines specify a SINGLE 2-g dose 30-60 minutes prior to the procedure.

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 1 g infusion starting 2 hours prior to the procedure for all patients with mechanical valves
options.explanation: Intravenous vancomycin is reserved only for patients unable to take oral medications with severe penicillin anaphylaxis; oral amoxicillin is the standard first-line agent.

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 2 g administered as a single dose 30 to 60 minutes prior to the dental procedure
options.explanation: INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS (IE) ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS guidelines (AHA/ACC) were substantially updated to restrict prophylaxis strictly to PATIENTS AT THE HIGHEST RISK OF ADVERSE OUTCOMES from endocarditis undergoing HIGH-RISK PROCEDURES. Antibiotic prophylaxis is INDICATED ONLY IF BOTH criteria are met: (1) CRITERION 1: HIGH-RISK CARDIAC CONDITION: (a) PROSTHETIC CARDIAC VALVES (mechanical or bioprosthetic, or transcatheter valves [TAVR]); (b) Prosthetic material used for cardiac valve repair (annuloplasty rings/clips); (c) PREVIOUS HISTORY OF INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS; (d) UNREPAIRED CYANOTIC CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE (including palliative shunts/conduits); (e) Completely repaired congenital heart defect with prosthetic material during the first 6 months post-procedure; (f) Repaired congenital heart disease with residual defects adjacent to prosthetic patch/device; (g) CARDIAC TRANSPLANT RECIPIENTS WHO DEVELOP CARDIAC VALVULOPATHY. (Prophylaxis is NO LONGER recommended for native valve disease, bicuspid aortic valve, mitral valve prolapse, or acquired rheumatic heart disease). (2) CRITERION 2: HIGH-RISK PROCEDURE: Dental procedures that involve MANIPULATION OF GINGIVAL TISSUE or the PERIAPICAL REGION OF TEETH, OR PERFORATION OF THE ORAL MUCOSA (e.g., tooth extraction, scaling, periodontal surgery). (Prophylaxis is NOT recommended for routine non-bleeding restorative dentistry, fillings, or gastrointestinal/genitourinary procedures). PROPHYLAXIS REGIMEN: The standard first-line regimen for patients who can tolerate oral medications is A SINGLE ORAL DOSE OF AMOXICILLIN 2 G ADMINISTERED 30 TO 60 MINUTES BEFORE THE PROCEDURE (targets viridans group streptococci). For patients allergic to penicillin: CEPHALEXIN 2 g (if non-anaphylactic), OR AZITHROMYCIN/CLARITHROMYCIN 500 mg, OR DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg (clindamycin is no longer recommended due to high risk of C. difficile). If unable to take oral medication: Ampicillin 2 g IM/IV or Cefazolin 1 g IM/IV.

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose 1 hour prior to the procedure
options.explanation: Ciprofloxacin has poor activity against oral viridans group streptococci (the primary pathogen in dental bacteremia) and is not an approved prophylactic agent.

topic: Complete Hydatidiform Mole Suction D&C and Serial beta-hCG Surveillance
stem: A 24-year-old primigravida presents to the clinic with dark brown vaginal bleeding ('prune-juice' discharge) and severe, intractable nausea and vomiting (hyperemesis gravidarum) at 11 weeks of gestation based on her last menstrual period. Over the past 2 weeks, she has noted rapid abdominal enlargement. Physical examination reveals an alert woman. Vital signs: blood pressure 152/94 mm Hg, heart rate 104/min, and afebrile. Abdominal examination reveals a non-tender, soft uterine fundus that is palpable at the level of the umbilicus, consistent with a 20-week gestation (uterine size significantly greater than dates). Pelvic speculum examination reveals dark blood in the vaginal vault without active tissue passage, and bimanual examination confirms an enlarged uterus with bilateral, non-tender, cystic, mobile adnexal masses measuring approximately 6 cm (theca lutein cysts). Quantitative serum beta-hCG is markedly elevated at 285,000 mIU/mL (expected at 11 weeks < 100,000 mIU/mL). Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrates a complete absence of an embryo, fetus, or amniotic sac, with the uterine cavity completely distended by a heterogeneous, echogenic mass containing innumerable small, anechoic cystic spaces with acoustic enhancement ('snowstorm' or 'cluster-of-grapes' appearance). Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan for this patient?

options.text: Immediate administration of systemic intramuscular methotrexate monotherapy without surgical uterine evacuation
options.explanation: Methotrexate is indicated for malignant Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia (choriocarcinoma, persistently elevated beta-hCG post-evacuation), not for initial uncomplicated hydatidiform mole, which requires surgical evacuation via suction D&C.

options.text: Immediate total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy including removal of the theca lutein cysts
options.explanation: Hysterectomy is reserved only for women who have completed childbearing; removing theca lutein cysts is inappropriate because they regress spontaneously once beta-hCG drops.

options.text: Expectant management with serial transvaginal ultrasound every 2 weeks because moles frequently resorb spontaneously
options.explanation: Expectant management carries high risks of life-threatening uterine hemorrhage, invasive mole, and choriocarcinoma; immediate suction D&C is mandatory.

options.text: Oral mifepristone followed by misoprostol medical abortion in the outpatient setting
options.explanation: Medical evacuation with prostaglandins is strictly avoided in complete molar pregnancies due to high risks of incomplete evacuation, severe hemorrhage, and trophoblastic embolization.

options.text: Suction dilation and curettage (D&C), baseline chest radiography, and serial weekly serum quantitative beta-hCG monitoring until undetectable for 3 consecutive weeks, followed by monthly monitoring for 6 months while maintaining strict reliable contraception
options.explanation: GESTATIONAL TROPHOBLASTIC DISEASE (GTD) encompasses a spectrum of tumors arising from placental trophoblastic epithelium: (1) COMPLETE HYDATIDIFORM MOLE: Results from fertilization of an 'empty' enucleated ovum by a single sperm that duplicates its chromosomes (46,XX, 90%) or by two sperm (46,XY, 10%). Gross pathology shows diffuse, generalized hydropic swelling of all chorionic villi with marked trophoblastic hyperplasia, forming macroscopic translucent vesicles ('cluster of grapes'). Chromosomes are purely paternal (diploid androgenesis). Embryonic tissue is COMPLETELY ABSENT. (2) PARTIAL HYDATIDIFORM MOLE: Results from fertilization of a normal ovum by two sperm (triploid 69,XXY, 69,XXX), featuring focal hydropic villi and fetal parts/embryonic tissue. CLINICAL PRESENTATION OF COMPLETE MOLE: Vaginal bleeding ('prune juice' appearance), UTERINE ENLARGEMENT GREATER THAN DATES, hyperemesis gravidarum, early-onset PREECLAMPSIA (< 20 weeks of gestation, a classic boards giveaway), hyperthyroidism (high beta-hCG cross-reacts with TSH receptors), and BILATERAL THECA LUTEIN CYSTS (ovarian hyperstimulation from extreme beta-hCG). Classic ultrasound shows a 'SNOWSTORM' or 'BUNCH OF GRAPES' appearance without a fetus. MANAGEMENT PROTOCOL: (1) PRIMARY TREATMENT: SUCTION DILATION AND CURETTAGE (D&C) is the definitive method of uterine evacuation for patients desiring fertility preservation; (2) BASELINE CHEST RADIOGRAPHY: To rule out pulmonary metastases (lungs are the most common site of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia / choriocarcinoma); (3) POST-EVACUATION SURVEILLANCE: SERIAL SERUM QUANTITATIVE BETA-HCG MUST BE MONITORED WEEKLY until levels become undetectable (< 5 mIU/mL) for 3 consecutive weeks, followed by MONTHLY MONITORING FOR 6 MONTHS. (4) MANDATORY CONTRACEPTION: The patient must maintain STRICT, RELIABLE CONTRACEPTION (oral contraceptives or barrier methods) for the entire 6 months because pregnancy would elevate beta-hCG, making it impossible to differentiate gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (choriocarcinoma/invasive mole) from a normal pregnancy.

subject: Surgery
topic: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Screening and Surgical Repair Indications
stem: A 68-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a Medicare annual wellness visit. He is completely asymptomatic, reports no abdominal, back, or flank pain, and has no personal history of cardiovascular disease. He smoked 1.5 packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years before quitting 2 years ago (60-pack-year smoking history). Physical examination reveals a pleasant, healthy-appearing man. Vital signs: blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg and heart rate 72/min. Abdominal examination demonstrates a non-tender, soft abdomen with a prominent, pulsatile, expansile mass palpated in the epigastric and periumbilical region measuring approximately 4.5 cm in width. Peripheral pulses are normal and equal bilaterally. Transthoracic screening ultrasound of the abdominal aorta confirms an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) measuring 4.6 cm in maximal outer-to-outer transverse diameter. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan for this patient?

options.text: Serial abdominal aortic ultrasonography surveillance every 6 to 12 months, aggressive cardiovascular risk factor modification (smoking cessation, statin, blood pressure control), with elective repair indicated if diameter reaches >= 5.5 cm or expands > 0.5 cm in 6 months
options.explanation: ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM (AAA) is defined as a focal, permanent dilation of the abdominal aorta to >= 3.0 CM (or > 50% increase compared to normal diameter). More than 90% are INFRARENAL (arising below the renal arteries). The single strongest, most significant modifiable risk factor is CIGARETTE SMOKING (risk increases 5-fold, with a strong dose-dependent relationship), followed by advanced age (> 65), male sex (4:1 male-to-female ratio), white race, hypertension, atherosclerosis, and family history. topic: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip Screening Ultrasound and Pavlik Harness
stem: A 4-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for a well-child examination. She was born at 39 weeks of gestation via scheduled cesarean delivery due to persistent breech presentation. Pregnancy was uncomplicated, and there is no family history of early hip disease. On physical examination, the infant is calm and cooperative. Examination of the lower extremities reveals asymmetric thigh and gluteal skin folds. With the infant lying supine and hips flexed to 90 degrees, the pediatrician places the thumb on the inner thigh and fingers over the greater trochanter and gently abducts the left hip while applying anterior pressure to the greater trochanter. A distinct, palpable, non-acoustic clunk is felt as the left femoral head relocates into the acetabulum (positive Ortolani sign). Subsequent adduction of the left hip with gentle posterior pressure elicits a palpable subluxation of the femoral head out of the acetabulum (positive Barlow sign). The right hip examination is completely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnostic imaging and initial management?

options.text: Obtain immediate anteroposterior pelvic radiographs to measure the acetabular angle and Hilgenreiner line
options.explanation: Plain radiographs are unreliable and uninformative in infants < 4-6 months because the femoral head and acetabulum are cartilaginous and unossified; ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice.

options.text: Perform dynamic bilateral hip ultrasonography, and initiate treatment with a Pavlik harness to maintain the hips in flexion and abduction
options.explanation: DEVELOPMENTAL DYSPLASIA OF THE HIP (DDH) is a spectrum of congenital hip instability ranging from mild acetabular dysplasia to complete dislocated femoral head. Major risk factors include: BREECH PRESENTATION (the strongest risk factor, present in this patient), FEMALE SEX (80% of cases, due to maternal relaxin sensitivity), FIRST-BORN INFANT, OLIGOHYDRAMNIOS, and POSITIVE FAMILY HISTORY. CLINICAL SCREENING MANEUVERS (performed at every newborn and well-child visit until walking age): (1) ORTOLANI MANEUVER: With the hip flexed to 90 degrees, the examiner gently abducts the thigh while lifting the greater trochanter anteriorly; a palpable 'CLUNK' indicates REDUCTION of a dislocated femoral head into the acetabulum (positive Ortolani = dislocated hip that is reducible). (2) BARLOW MANEUVER: The examiner adducts the flexed hip and applies gentle posterior pressure on the inner thigh; a palpable clunk/jolt indicates POSTERIOR SUBLUXATION/DISLOCATION of an unstable hip out of the acetabulum (positive Barlow = dislocatable hip). Asymmetric skin folds or leg length discrepancy (Galeazzi sign) are secondary findings. IMAGING MODALITY SELECTION: (1) INFANTS < 4 TO 6 MONTHS OF AGE: ULTRASONOGRAPHY OF THE HIPS is the imaging modality of choice because the femoral head and acetabulum are composed entirely of radiolucent cartilaginous tissue and are INVISIBLE ON PLAIN RADIOGRAPHS. (Hip ultrasound is routinely scheduled at 4-6 weeks for high-risk infants [e.g., breech girls] to avoid false positives from transient physiological newborn ligamentous laxity). (2) INFANTS >= 4 TO 6 MONTHS OF AGE: PLAIN ANTEROPOSTERIOR HIP RADIOGRAPHY is appropriate once the femoral head ossification center has developed. INITIAL MANAGEMENT: The FIRST-LINE TREATMENT for reducible DDH diagnosed in infants < 6 months of age is a PAVLIK HARNESS. The Pavlik harness is a dynamic flexion-abduction orthosis that holds the hips in FLEXION (90-100 degrees) AND MODERATE ABDOMINAL ABDUCTION (45-60 degrees), directing the femoral head centrally into the acetabulum to stimulate normal concentric acetabular remodeling. It achieves > 90% success.

options.text: Immediate closed reduction under general anesthesia and placement of a rigid hip spica cast
options.explanation: Closed reduction and spica casting are reserved for infants > 6 months of age or those who fail dynamic Pavlik harness therapy; Pavlik harness is the non-invasive first-line therapy.

options.explanation: A palpable Ortolani clunk represents true joint dislocation, not benign ligamentous clicking; delaying treatment past 6 months leads to permanent acetabular dysplasia, limb shortening, and waddling gait.

subject: Medicine
topic: Solitary Pulmonary Nodule Fleischner Guidelines and PET-CT Biopsy
stem: A 66-year-old man presents to the pulmonary clinic for evaluation of an incidental lung nodule discovered during a non-contrast chest CT performed for evaluation of rib trauma following a minor fall. He is completely asymptomatic, has no cough, hemoptysis, shortness of breath, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and continues to smoke half a pack daily. Chest CT demonstrates a solitary, non-calcified, solid pulmonary nodule in the right upper lobe measuring 14 mm (1.4 cm) in maximal diameter. The nodule displays irregular, spiculated margins and is surrounded by minimal ground-glass attenuation; there is no mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Review of the electronic medical record reveals no previous chest imaging for comparison. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Serial non-contrast chest CT surveillance in 12 months because the nodule is less than 20 mm in diameter
options.explanation: A 14-mm spiculated nodule in an active 40-pack-year smoker has an 70-80% malignancy probability; delaying evaluation for 12 months allows curable early-stage lung cancer to metastasize.

options.text: Initiation of a 2-week course of oral levofloxacin and repeat chest radiograph to evaluate for infectious resolution
options.explanation: Empiric antibiotics in asymptomatic patients with suspicious pulmonary nodules delay cancer diagnosis without benefit and are explicitly discouraged by guidelines.

options.text: Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) or tissue biopsy (transthoracic needle biopsy or bronchoscopy), followed by surgical wedge resection if malignancy is confirmed
options.explanation: A SOLITARY PULMONARY NODULE (SPN) is defined as a single, discrete, rounded, well-demarcated parenchymal opacity measuring <= 30 MM (3.0 cm) in diameter, completely surrounded by normal aerated lung tissue, without atelectasis, hilar enlargement, or pleural effusion. (Lesions > 30 mm are classified as 'lung masses' and are malignant in > 80% of cases). When evaluating an SPN: (1) STEP 1: COMPARE WITH HISTORICAL CHEST RADIOGRAPHS OR CT SCANS. Absence of growth over a 2-year period confirms benign etiology (granuloma, hamartoma), requiring no further workup. (2) STEP 2: ASSESS CLINICAL AND RADIOLOGICAL MALIGNANCY RISK: (a) HIGH-RISK FEATURES: Age > 65 years, CURRENT OR HEAVY SMOKING HISTORY (> 30 pack-years), personal history of cancer, NODULE SIZE > 8-10 MM (cancer risk increases directly with diameter: < 5 mm [< 1%], 5-10 mm [6-28%], > 20 mm [> 64-80%]), SPICULATED OR CORONA RADIATA MARGINS (spiculation reflects malignant lymphatic infiltration), UPPER LOBE LOCATION, and SOLID OR PART-SOLID ATTENUATION. (b) LOW-RISK/BENIGN FEATURES: Age < 35, non-smoker, smooth sharp margins, size < 6 mm, and BENIGN CALCIFICATION PATTERNS (diffuse dense, central bull's-eye, laminated/concentric, or popcorn calcification [hamartoma]). (3) STEP 3: MANAGEMENT BASED ON RISK CATEGORY (FLEISCHNER SOCIETY / ACCP GUIDELINES): (a) LOW RISK (< 5% risk, nodules < 6-8 mm in young non-smokers): Serial low-dose surveillance CT at 6-12 months. (b) INTERMEDIATE RISK (5-65% risk, nodules > 8 mm without definitive features): 18F-FLUORODEOXYGLUCOSE (FDG) PET-CT SCAN. Hypermetabolic uptake (SUV > 2.5) indicates high malignancy risk warranting tissue biopsy. (c) HIGH RISK (> 65% risk: 14-mm spiculated upper lobe nodule in an active elderly smoker): The estimated pretest probability of malignancy is > 70-80%. Guidelines recommend FDG PET-CT FOR METABOLIC STAGING OR DIRECT TISSUE BIOPSY (percutaneous CT-guided core biopsy or bronchoscopy with radial EBUS) OR SURGICAL RESECTION (video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery [VATS] wedge resection) with intraoperative frozen section.

options.text: Perform an emergent right pneumonectomy under general anesthesia without prior staging or frozen section
options.explanation: Pneumonectomy is excessive and morbid for a 1.4-cm peripheral nodule; sublobar wedge resection or lobectomy after biopsy/staging is the appropriate oncological standard.

options.text: Serum measurement of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and neuron-specific enolase (NSE) to determine if resection is required
options.explanation: Serum tumor markers lack sensitivity and specificity for early solitary pulmonary nodules and have zero role in screening or management decisions.

subject: Neurology
topic: Bell Palsy Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron Facial Palsy Corticosteroids
stem: A 42-year-old previously healthy man presents to the clinic with an acute onset of right-sided facial weakness that began 24 hours ago. He noticed difficulty closing his right eye while shaving this morning and states that coffee leaks from the right corner of his mouth when drinking. He also reports increased sensitivity to everyday loud noises in his right ear (hyperacusis) and noticed that food tastes strange on the anterior portion of his tongue. Physical examination reveals an alert man. Neurological examination of the face demonstrates: flattening of the right nasolabial fold, drooping of the right corner of the mouth with inability to smile or whistle on the right, and INABILITY TO RAISE THE RIGHT EYEBROW OR WRINKLE THE RIGHT FOREHEAD. When asked to close his eyes tightly, the right eyelid fails to close completely (lagophthalmos), and the right eyeball rolls upward and outward (Bell phenomenon). Sensory examination of the face to light touch is completely normal across all three trigeminal divisions. Hearing is intact to finger rub, and examination of the external auditory canal reveals no vesicles or erythema. Extraocular eye movements, arm and leg motor strength, and deep tendon reflexes are completely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Perform an emergent non-contrast head CT and prepare for intravenous alteplase thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke
options.explanation: The patient has forehead involvement (inability to wrinkle forehead), which confirms a peripheral lower motor neuron lesion (Bell palsy), definitively ruling out an upper motor neuron cortical stroke.

options.text: Initiation of oral valacyclovir monotherapy without corticosteroids
options.explanation: Antiviral monotherapy has no proven efficacy in Bell palsy; systemic corticosteroids (prednisone) are the proven first-line therapy.

options.text: Immediate surgical decompression of the facial nerve in the fallopian canal
options.explanation: Surgical nerve decompression is not recommended for acute Bell palsy due to high risks of permanent sensorineural hearing loss without proven benefit over medical steroids.

options.text: Initiation of oral prednisone (60 mg daily for 7 to 10 days) started within 72 hours of symptom onset, accompanied by lubricating artificial tears and an eye patch at night to prevent corneal abrasion
options.explanation: BELL PALSY is an acute, unilateral peripheral lower motor neuron facial nerve (CRANIAL NERVE VII) palsy, thought to arise from viral reactivation (most commonly Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1, HSV-1) causing inflammation, edema, and mechanical compression of the facial nerve within the narrow labyrinthine segment of the fallopian canal. CRITICAL CLINICAL DIFFERENTIATION: (1) LOWER MOTOR NEURON (LMN) FACIAL NERVE LESION (Bell palsy, Lyme disease, acoustic neuroma, parotid tumor): Involves the entire facial nerve nucleus or peripheral nerve. Because the upper facial motor nucleus receives bilateral cortical input, but the lower motor nerve carries fibers to all facial muscles, an LMN LESION CAUSES PARALYSIS OF THE ENTIRE IPSILATERAL HALF OF THE FACE, INCLUDING INABILITY TO WRINKLE THE FOREHEAD OR RAISE THE EYEBROW. (2) UPPER MOTOR NEURON (UMN) CORTICOBULBAR LESION (Stroke, brain tumor): Lesion is in the motor cortex or internal capsule. Because the motor neurons that innervate the FOREHEAD receive BILATERAL CORTICOBULBAR INNERVATION from both cerebral hemispheres, an UMN stroke SPARES THE FOREHEAD (the patient CAN still wrinkle the forehead and raise both eyebrows, with paralysis restricted to the lower two-thirds of the contralateral face). Associated facial nerve findings: Hyperacusis (loss of stapedius muscle dampening via nerve to stapedius), loss of taste on anterior 2/3 of tongue (chorda tympani), and impaired lacrimation/salivation. MANAGEMENT: (1) SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROIDS: ORAL PREDNISONE (60-80 mg daily for 7-10 days) STARTED WITHIN 72 HOURS OF ONSET significantly accelerates and increases the rate of complete facial motor recovery. (Antivirals [valacyclovir] provide minimal added benefit, indicated only in severe paralysis). (2) EYE CARE IS PARAMOUNT: Inability to close the eyelid (lagophthalmos) exposes the cornea to desiccation, keratitis, and permanent corneal ulceration; frequent daytime LUBRICATING ARTIFICIAL TEARS, lubricating ophthalmic ointment at bedtime, and TAPING THE EYELID SHUT / EYE PATCH AT NIGHT are mandatory.

options.explanation: Bell palsy is not bacterial otitis; failure to provide eye lubrication and night patching leads to severe corneal ulceration and permanent vision loss.

topic: SIADH Euvolemic Hyponatremia Fluid Restriction and Safe Sodium Correction
stem: A 68-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history is hospitalized for evaluation of a newly diagnosed left hilar lung mass. Over the past 48 hours, he has developed mild fatigue, anorexia, headache, and subtle cognitive slowing. Physical examination reveals an alert, oriented man with normal skin turgor, moist oral mucous membranes, flat neck veins, normal blood pressure (128/78 mm Hg), and completely ABSENT PERIPHERAL EDEMA or ascites (clinically euvolemic). Laboratory evaluation reveals: serum sodium 118 mEq/L (normal 135-145 mEq/L), serum potassium 4.2 mEq/L, serum chloride 86 mEq/L, serum bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 8 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. Measured serum osmolality is low at 246 mOsm/kg H2O (normal 275-295 mOsm/kg). Spot urine studies demonstrate: urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg H2O (inappropriately elevated in the presence of hypoosmolar plasma), and spot urine sodium 54 mEq/L (normal < 20 mEq/L in hypovolemia). Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and morning cortisol are completely normal. Chest CT confirms a 4.2-cm left hilar mass invading the main bronchus with mediastinal adenopathy, and bronchoscopic biopsy confirms small cell lung carcinoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient's hyponatremia?

options.text: Vigorous intravenous infusion of 0.9% normal saline at 250 mL/hr to rapidly correct the serum sodium deficit
options.explanation: Administering normal saline in SIADH is a classic error that WORSENS HYPONATREMIA: the kidney excretes the infused sodium in concentrated urine while retaining the free water, driving serum sodium lower.

options.text: Rapid intravenous infusion of 3% hypertonic saline to raise serum sodium by 18 mEq/L over the first 12 hours
options.explanation: Correcting chronic hyponatremia by > 8 mEq/L in 24 hours triggers fatal osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) and locked-in syndrome.

options.text: Initiation of high-dose intravenous desmopressin (dDAVP) and free water oral loading
options.explanation: Desmopressin is a synthetic ADH analog; giving it in SIADH hyperstimulates V2 receptors, accelerating water retention and fatal cerebral edema.

options.text: Immediate administration of intravenous fludrocortisone 2 mg bolus as monotherapy
options.explanation: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid used for cerebral salt wasting (hypovolemic hyponatremia), not euvolemic SIADH.

options.text: Fluid restriction to < 800 to 1,000 mL/day as first-line therapy, with a strict maximum rate of sodium correction not exceeding 8 mEq/L in any 24-hour period to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome
options.explanation: SYNDROME OF INAPPROPRIATE ANTIDIURETIC HORMONE SECRETION (SIADH) is characterized by autonomous, uninhibited release of vasopressin (ADH) independent of plasma osmolality or volume status. Etiologies include: (1) Central nervous system disorders (stroke, trauma, meningitis); (2) Malignancy (PARANEOPLASTIC SECRETION BY SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER, the prototype cause); (3) Pulmonary infections (pneumonia, TB); (4) Medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide). Pathophysiology: Persistent ADH binds V2 receptors in collecting ducts, causing continuous aquaporin-2 insertion and water reabsorption. Water retention expands extracellular fluid volume, suppressing aldosterone and stimulating natriuretic peptides (ANP/BNP), which promotes urinary sodium excretion (natriuresis). The resulting state is CLINICALLY EUVOLEMIC HYPOTONIC HYPONATREMIA. Diagnostic criteria: (a) Decreased effective serum osmolality (< 275 mOsm/kg); (b) Inappropriately concentrated urine (Urine Osm > 100 mOsm/kg, usually > 300); (c) Inappropriately high urinary sodium excretion (Urine Na > 30-40 mEq/L) despite hyponatremia; (d) Clinical euvolemia (no edema, normal BP/JVD); (e) Normal thyroid (ruling out hypothyroidism) and normal adrenal function (ruling out adrenal insufficiency). MANAGEMENT: (1) ASYMPTOMATIC OR MILD-TO-MODERATE SIADH: The FIRST-LINE TREATMENT IS FLUID RESTRICTION (restricting total daily fluid intake to < 800-1,000 mL/day). Second-line therapies include oral sodium chloride tablets plus low-dose loop diuretics (furosemide to wash out medullary gradient), oral urea, or vasopressin receptor antagonists (vaptans: tolvaptan). (2) SEVERE SYMPTOMATIC SIADH (seizures, coma, severe obtundation): Hypertonic 3% saline (100 mL bolus) is indicated. CRITICAL SAFETY RULE: IN CHRONIC HYPONATREMIA (> 48 HOURS), THE RATE OF SODIUM CORRECTION MUST NEVER EXCEED 8 MEQ/L IN ANY 24-HOUR PERIOD (or 6-8 mEq/L per day). Correcting chronic hyponatremia too rapidly causes rapid brain cell dehydration and destruction of oligodendrocytes, precipitating irreversible, fatal OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION SYNDROME (ODS / central pontine myelinolysis), presenting with spastic quadriparesis, pseudobulbar palsy, and 'locked-in' syndrome.
